evidence: This sequence appears to be human LRP4, an LDL-receptor family member that acts as the agrin receptor/MuSK co-receptor and binds Wnt-pathway antagonists such as sclerostin and DKK1; from recall, its known ligands are proteins and I am not aware of evidence for direct cholesterol binding.

The sequence looks like human LRP4 (LDLR class A repeats, EGF modules, four YWTD beta-propellers, single transmembrane helix), which binds agrin and bridges it to the kinase MuSK at the neuromuscular junction; this is consistent with an adaptor role, though I am inferring it from recalled biology rather than a confirmed annotation.

This is LRP4, a single-pass cell-surface receptor (LDLR class A repeats, EGF-like domains, YWTD beta-propellers) that binds agrin, MuSK and sclerostin at the plasma membrane; it has no chromatin-related domains and no known nucleosome-binding role.

This looks like human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), a soluble short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase-fold enzyme with no signal peptide or transmembrane anchor; from recall it has no Golgi annotation, unlike the membrane-anchored Golgi relative UXS1.

This looks like human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase family nucleotide-sugar dehydratase; as far as I recall it is annotated for nucleotide-sugar metabolism rather than glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis, though a link to proteoglycan synthesis (Catel-Manzke syndrome) has been proposed, so this is not certain.

The sequence matches human TGDS, annotated as a dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase, and it retains the NAD-binding glycine motif (GGAGFIASH), the TDE catalytic triad and the YxxxK motif typical of RmlB-type enzymes. This rests on homology rather than direct assay, and I recall recent work suggesting its physiological substrate may be UDP-glucose instead.

This sequence matches human TGDS, an SDR-family NDP-sugar 4,6-dehydratase historically named dTDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase; humans do not make dTDP-glucose, and I recall recent work reporting that it acts on UDP-glucose to form UDP-4-keto-6-deoxyglucose, though this rests on memory of that literature rather than on the sequence alone.

This sequence appears to be human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase-fold enzyme linked to Catel-Manzke syndrome; from recall, I know of no evidence or annotation placing it in the photoreceptor inner segment.

This sequence looks like human TGDS (dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase), a short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase-fold enzyme with an N-terminal NAD-binding GxxGxxG motif that acts in nucleotide-sugar metabolism; I know of no evidence linking it to cell surface receptor signaling.

The sequence looks like human dTDP-D-glucose 4,6-dehydratase (TGDS), a soluble NAD-dependent epimerase/dehydratase with an N-terminal GxxGxxG Rossmann motif and no seven-transmembrane GPCR architecture; this identification is from sequence features and recall, and bile acid receptor activity belongs to GPBAR1/TGR5, not this protein.

The sequence is human fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (ALDOA), a glycolytic enzyme whose known annotations cover glycolysis, fructose metabolism and actin/cytoskeletal roles; from recall, it is not specifically annotated with positive regulation of glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

The sequence is human fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (ALDOA), a glycolytic/gluconeogenic enzyme that cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate; from recall, it has no known role in glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis.

The sequence is human fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (ALDOA), a glycolytic enzyme; from recall of its known annotations (glycolysis, actin binding, platelet degranulation) it has no established role in positively regulating TLR9 signaling.

The sequence matches human fructose-bisphosphate aldolase A (ALDOA), a core glycolytic enzyme that cleaves fructose-1,6-bisphosphate; I recall no evidence or annotation linking it to toxic metabolite repair, though this rests on recognising the sequence from memory.

The sequence is human myeloperoxidase (MPO), which is reported to bind chromatin and drive its decondensation during neutrophil extracellular trap formation; from what I recall of recent structural work (not verified here), it binds nucleosomes directly and destabilises them, consistent with nucleosome disassembly.

The sequence is human myeloperoxidase (MPO); it binds chromatin during neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and I recall recent structural work showing direct MPO–nucleosome binding, though this is from memory rather than a checked annotation.

This is human myeloperoxidase; beyond its peroxidase activity it has been reported to bind chromatin and promote its decondensation during neutrophil extracellular trap formation, and to trigger release of neutrophil elastase from the azurosome complex, which fits a complex-destabilizing role. This rests on recalled literature rather than a confirmed annotation, so confidence is moderate.

The sequence is human myeloperoxidase (MPO), a secreted/azurophil-granule heme peroxidase of neutrophils that generates hypochlorous acid for microbial killing; it has no known role in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.
This sequence is human myeloperoxidase, a secreted heme peroxidase of the animal peroxidase family that generates hypochlorous acid in neutrophils; it has no CoA/thiol ligase domain or activity.

The sequence is recognisable from memory as human myeloperoxidase, a secreted heme peroxidase of neutrophil granules; its known molecular functions are peroxidase activity and heme/heparin binding, not bridging proteins to other macromolecules as an adaptor.

This is human LAMP2 (the LAMP2A isoform, judging by the C-terminal GLKHHHAGYEQF tail), the lysosomal receptor for chaperone-mediated autophagy; from recalled literature rather than a confirmed annotation, LAMP2A-dependent degradation of GPX4 promotes ferroptosis, so the term plausibly applies.

This is human LAMP2 (the LAMP2A isoform, ending in the KHHHAGYEQF cytosolic tail), a lysosomal membrane glycoprotein involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy and lysosome/autophagosome function, not in adenylate cyclase-activating GPCR signalling.

This is human LAMP2 (lysosome-associated membrane glycoprotein 2, LAMP-2A isoform with the C-terminal KHHHAGYEQF tail), a lysosomal membrane protein involved in chaperone-mediated autophagy and lysosome function, not a component of the intraflagellar transport machinery.

The sequence is human LAMP2 (isoform LAMP-2A, with the C-terminal GLKHHHAGYEQF tail), a lysosomal membrane glycoprotein that acts as the receptor for chaperone-mediated autophagy and in autophagosome-lysosome fusion. It is not a mitochondrial carrier; mitochondrial CoA transport is performed by SLC25 family members such as SLC25A42, so this is a judgement from recalled function rather than a checked annotation.

The sequence matches human SLC25A16 (Graves disease carrier protein), a mitochondrial inner-membrane carrier and ortholog of yeast Leu5 that is thought to import coenzyme A into the matrix; this rests on recalled homology and complementation evidence rather than direct transport assays.

This sequence is a human mitochondrial solute carrier family member (it matches SLC25A16, the Graves disease carrier protein, as far as I can recall), an inner-membrane transporter with no known role in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.

The sequence appears to be SLC25A16 (Graves disease carrier protein), a mitochondrial inner-membrane solute carrier of the SLC25 family thought to transport coenzyme A; from what I recall it is not a GPCR pathway component and has no role in adenylate cyclase-activating signalling.

The sequence looks like human SLC25A16 (Graves disease carrier protein), a mitochondrial inner-membrane carrier linked to coenzyme A transport; I recall no evidence tying it to glucose-stimulated insulin secretion, unlike SLC25A22.

The sequence is human spleen tyrosine kinase SYK (tandem SH2 domains plus a C-terminal tyrosine kinase domain); published work reports SYK is required for CpG/TLR9-driven activation in B cells and phosphorylates TLR9. This is recalled from the literature rather than a confirmed GO annotation, so confidence is moderate.
This is human ZAP-70, a tandem-SH2 cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase that acts in T-cell receptor signalling; it has no known role in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.
This is human spleen tyrosine kinase SYK (tandem SH2 domains plus a tyrosine kinase domain), which acts in immunoreceptor signalling, not in ribosome-associated mRNA surveillance or non-stop decay.

This sequence is human spleen tyrosine kinase SYK (tandem SH2 domains plus a tyrosine kinase domain), a non-receptor kinase in immunoreceptor signalling; it is not a metabolite repair enzyme and has no known role in toxic metabolite repair.

The sequence matches human beta-arrestin 1 (ARRB1), whose known roles are GPCR desensitisation/internalisation and signalling scaffolding (ERK, NF-kappaB, ubiquitination); from recall, it has a link to GLP-1-stimulated insulin secretion but I am not aware of a specific annotation to intracellular glucose homeostasis.

The sequence is human beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), an adaptor that binds activated G protein-coupled receptors at the plasma membrane, mediating their desensitization and internalization and scaffolding downstream signalling such as ERK1/2 activation. This places it within cell surface receptor signalling; the call rests on recognising the protein from memory, not on a checked annotation record.

The sequence matches human beta-arrestin-1 (ARRB1), a GPCR desensitisation/endocytosis adaptor and signalling scaffold; from recall, its ciliary links are to Smoothened entry into cilia and (mainly beta-arrestin-2) GPCR removal, and it is not an IFT-A/dynein-2 retrograde transport component.

The sequence is human beta-arrestin 1 (ARRB1); beta-arrestins mediate removal of the GPCR GPR161 from the primary cilium membrane on Smoothened activation, which fits this term. This is from recall of the literature, not a checked annotation record.

This sequence is human beta-arrestin 1 (ARRB1), a cytosolic adaptor that mediates GPCR desensitization, internalization and signalling scaffolding; it has no known enzymatic or direct role in glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis.
The sequence is human beta-arrestin 1 (ARRB1), a GPCR desensitization and signalling scaffold/adaptor protein with no enzymatic or known role in malate metabolism.

The sequence is human beta-arrestin 2 (ARRB2), a cytosolic adaptor for GPCR desensitization, internalization and signalling scaffolding; from recall of its known roles, it has no established part in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.

The sequence is human GSK3B (glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta), a serine/threonine kinase known for roles in glycogen metabolism, Wnt signalling and tau phosphorylation; from recall, it carries no annotation for regulation of cholesterol transport.

This is human GSK3B (glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta), a Ser/Thr kinase in Wnt, insulin and tau signalling; from recall, its cardiac annotations concern hypertrophy and heart development rather than regulation of heart rate, so this is a moderately confident no.

This sequence is human GSK3B (glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta), a Ser/Thr kinase acting in Wnt/beta-catenin signalling, glycogen metabolism and tau phosphorylation; from recall, it is not a known component of transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.

This is human GSK3B (glycogen synthase kinase-3 beta), a serine/threonine kinase of Wnt, insulin and tau signalling; from recall, its cilia links are regulatory (ciliogenesis, e.g. via DZIP1 phosphorylation), and it is not a component of the IFT-A/dynein-2 retrograde transport machinery.

The sequence matches human STK19 (the 254-residue isoform), which 2024 studies, as I recall them, identified as a transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair factor that contacts lesion-stalled RNA polymerase II together with CSA, UVSSA and TFIIH; this is from memory of the literature, not derived from the sequence itself.

I recognise this sequence as human STK19 (the 254-residue winged-helix form), which 2024 studies showed is a core TC-NER factor that associates with the CSA/UVSSA/Pol II complex at stalled polymerase and helps position TFIIH; this is from recall of the literature, not a lookup.

This appears to be human STK19 (254-residue winged-helix isoform), which I recall from recent cryo-EM work as joining the stalled RNA polymerase II elongation complex with CSA, UVSSA and ELOF1 in transcription-coupled repair. The verdict rests on that recollection rather than a confirmed annotation, so confidence is moderate.

This sequence matches human STK19 (the 254-aa form), a transcription-coupled nucleotide excision repair factor that recent studies report interacts with and helps position TFIIH at lesion-stalled RNA Pol II; this is recalled from the literature rather than derived from the sequence.

This sequence matches human STK19 (the 254-residue isoform), a small winged-helix nucleic-acid-binding protein implicated in transcription-coupled DNA repair and formerly annotated as a kinase; it has no adenylate-forming or CoA-ligase domain that would give acid-thiol ligase activity.

This sequence appears to be human STK19 (the nuclear protein once called serine/threonine kinase 19, now linked to transcription-coupled DNA repair); it lacks the NAD-binding Rossmann fold of short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase-type sugar nucleotide dehydratases and has no known UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity.

The sequence appears to be human STK19, a nuclear protein involved in transcription-coupled DNA repair (and reported NRAS phosphorylation); I recall no ciliary tip localisation or IFT/Hedgehog-related role for it.

The sequence appears to be the human mitochondrial NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase gamma subunit (IDH3G), a TCA-cycle enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix; from recall, its localization annotations are mitochondrial rather than photoreceptor inner segment specifically.

The sequence looks like IDH3G, the gamma subunit of mitochondrial NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase, a TCA-cycle enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix. I recall no established chromatin annotation for it, though some studies report nuclear pools of TCA enzymes, so this is a judgement from memory rather than a certainty.

This sequence matches human mitochondrial NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase gamma subunit (IDH3G), a TCA-cycle enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix with no transmembrane region or known endolysosomal membrane localisation.

The sequence matches human IDH3G, the gamma subunit of mitochondrial NAD-dependent isocitrate dehydrogenase, a TCA-cycle enzyme of the mitochondrial matrix; from recall, there is no known localisation to the ciliary tip, which is typical of IFT and Hedgehog-pathway proteins.

This sequence matches human SUCLG1, the shared alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA ligase, which pairs with the SUCLG2 beta subunit to form the GDP-forming enzyme (EC 6.2.1.4); the alpha subunit carries the CoA-binding site and the catalytic histidine that is phosphorylated during the reaction.

This is the human succinyl-CoA ligase alpha subunit (SUCLG1), which works in the TCA cycle on succinyl-CoA/succinate interconversion; from recall, its annotations cover succinate and succinyl-CoA metabolism rather than malate metabolism.

The sequence matches human SUCLG1, the mitochondrial succinyl-CoA ligase alpha subunit, which carries the CoA-binding site and the phosphohistidine catalytic motif (GHAGAII); succinate-CoA ligase activity is a child term of acid-thiol ligase activity. This is based on recognising the sequence, not on a database lookup.

This is human SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA ligase (ADP/GDP-forming); from what I recall of its annotation, its ligase activity is toward succinate, while malate-CoA ligase is a distinct enzyme of methylotrophic bacteria and is not known for this human protein.

This is human SUCLG1, the alpha subunit of mitochondrial succinyl-CoA ligase, a core TCA cycle enzyme; from recall, its known roles are in succinyl-CoA/succinate metabolism, and I know of no evidence for a dedicated toxic metabolite repair function.

This sequence is the human succinyl-CoA ligase alpha subunit (SUCLG1), a mitochondrial TCA-cycle enzyme subunit whose known role is catalytic (CoA binding and phosphohistidine catalysis with the beta subunits), not bridging other macromolecules. This is human SUCLG1, the mitochondrial succinyl-CoA ligase alpha subunit (CoA-binding/ATP-citrate lyase-like fold), a TCA-cycle enzyme with no known chromatin or nucleosome-binding domain or role.

This is human SUCLG1, the mitochondrial succinyl-CoA ligase alpha subunit, a matrix TCA-cycle enzyme that binds CoA and nucleotide; I know of no phosphoinositide-binding domain or evidence for PI(3,5)P2 binding, so this is a judgement from its recognised function rather than a checked annotation.

The sequence matches human VLDLR (very low-density lipoprotein receptor), with LDL-receptor class A repeats, a single transmembrane helix and an NPVY tail motif; from recall of the literature, VLDLR is an entry receptor for minor-group rhinoviruses and for alphaviruses such as Semliki Forest virus.

This sequence is the human very low-density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR), a membrane receptor with LDL-receptor class A repeats, EGF-like domains, a YWTD beta-propeller and an NPxY tail; it has no succinyl-CoA synthetase catalytic domains.

This is human VLDLR, a transmembrane LDL-receptor-family protein that works as an endocytic cargo/lipoprotein and reelin receptor; from recall, its annotated functions are receptor and ligand-binding activities rather than adaptor activity bridging macromolecules.

This sequence is the human very low-density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR), with LDL-receptor class A repeats, EGF-like domains, a YWTD beta-propeller, a transmembrane helix and an NPxY tail. It is an endocytic/reelin receptor with no short-chain dehydratase fold or NAD-binding motif, so it does not have UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity.

This sequence is human TRIM28 (KAP1), a KRAB-zinc-finger corepressor with RBCC, PHD and bromodomain regions that is recruited to chromatin and binds HP1, SETDB1 and NuRD to drive heterochromatin formation; this is recalled from knowledge of the protein rather than derived from the sequence alone.

This is human TRIM28 (KAP1), which I recognise from the sequence; its known roles are KRAB-zinc-finger corepressor activity, heterochromatin formation, SUMO/ubiquitin ligase activity and DNA repair. Although one report links it to dampening TNF-induced NF-kappaB transcriptional activity, from memory it is not annotated with negative regulation of canonical NF-kappaB signalling, so this is a moderately confident no.

This is human TRIM28 (KAP1), a nuclear transcriptional corepressor and E3 SUMO ligase associated with chromatin and heterochromatin; I know of no evidence placing it in the photoreceptor inner segment.

This sequence is TRIM28 (KAP1), a RING/B-box/coiled-coil/PHD-bromodomain transcriptional corepressor that localises to the nucleus and heterochromatin; I recall no Golgi localisation for it, and it has no signal peptide or transmembrane region.

This is human TRIM28 (KAP1), a nuclear RING/B-box/PHD-bromodomain corepressor and SUMO/ubiquitin ligase involved in KRAB-ZNF-mediated silencing and DNA repair; from recall, it has no known role in ciliary membrane protein trafficking.

The sequence appears to be human SKIV2L/SKIC2 (recognised from recall, not a database check), the DExH-box RNA helicase of the cytoplasmic SKI complex, which feeds mRNAs on stalled ribosomes to the exosome for 3'-5' decay, including non-stop decay.

The sequence appears to be human SKIV2L (SKI2W), the DEVH-box RNA helicase of the cytoplasmic Ski complex, whose known role is 3'-5' exosome-mediated mRNA decay and RNA surveillance; I recall no established role in cholesterol transport regulation, though this is from memory of its annotations rather than a checked record.

This is human SKIV2L (SKIC2), the SKI-complex 3'-5' RNA helicase that works with the cytoplasmic exosome in mRNA decay and ribosome-associated quality control; from recall, its known immune role is limiting RIG-I-like receptor/interferon responses, with no specific evidence for negative regulation of canonical NF-kappaB signalling.

This appears to be human SKIV2L/SKIC2, the Ski2-like RNA helicase of the cytoplasmic SKI complex that supports exosome-mediated 3'-5' mRNA decay; I recognise it from the sequence and know of no role for it in promoting smoothened (Hedgehog) signaling.

This looks like human ZFYVE26 (spastizin), a large FYVE-domain protein known from recall to bind PI3P and partners such as Beclin 1, SPG11, KIF13A and the AP-5 complex; I am not aware of evidence for self-association, so identical protein binding is unlikely to be annotated.

This appears to be human ZFYVE26 (spastizin/SPG15), a FYVE-domain protein that binds phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate and acts in cytokinesis, autophagy and lysosome reformation; I know of no evidence that it binds cholesterol.

This sequence appears to be human ZFYVE26 (spastizin/SPG15), a large FYVE zinc-finger protein that binds PI3P and acts in cytokinesis, autophagy and lysosome reformation; it has no adenylate-forming or CoA-ligase domain, so acid-thiol ligase activity is not expected.

This sequence appears to be human ZFYVE26 (spastizin, SPG15), a large FYVE zinc-finger protein involved in cytokinesis, autophagy and endolysosomal trafficking; it has no short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase-type NAD-binding dehydratase domain that UDP-glucose 4,6-dehydratase activity would require.

The sequence looks like human MRGPRE, a Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor; I recall it being linked, by similarity to the mouse ortholog, to islet hormone secretion and glucose homeostasis, though this is from memory and not certain.

The sequence looks like a human Mas-related G-protein coupled receptor (probably MRGPRG), a seven-transmembrane GPCR; such receptors are annotated to the plasma membrane as multi-pass membrane proteins, though this rests on family recognition from the sequence rather than direct evidence.

The sequence appears to be human MRGPRE, a Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor with seven transmembrane helices, so it is expected to signal from the plasma membrane; it is an orphan receptor, so this rests on family membership and recall rather than direct experimental evidence.
The sequence looks like human MRGPRE, an orphan Mas-related GPCR; from memory it has only generic GPCR-signalling annotation and no evidence of Gs/adenylate cyclase-activating coupling.

The sequence appears to be human MRGPRE, a Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor; I recall, without being certain, reports of Mas-related receptors D and E being expressed in pancreatic islets and modulating glucose-stimulated hormone secretion, so the annotation is plausible but this is a low-confidence call from memory.

The sequence appears to be human MRGPRE, an orphan Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor with no known bile acid ligand; within this family bile acid receptor activity has been shown for MRGPRX4 (and separately for GPBAR1/TGR5), not for MRGPRE. The sequence looks like a Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor (probably MRGPRE, judged from recall of length and sequence features), not the bile acid receptor GPBAR1/TGR5 that mediates this cAMP-linked pathway, and I know of no evidence linking this protein to bile acid signalling.

The sequence looks like a Mas-related G protein-coupled receptor (probably MRGPRE, identified from recall rather than a database lookup), a multi-pass plasma membrane receptor mainly associated with sensory neurons; I know of no evidence placing it in the photoreceptor inner segment.

The sequence appears to be a human Mas-related G-protein coupled receptor (most likely MRGPRE, an orphan seven-transmembrane receptor); its molecular function is GPCR signalling, not bridging macromolecules as an adaptor. The sequence looks like a human Mas-related G-protein coupled receptor (probably MRGPRE, an orphan sensory-neuron GPCR), identified from sequence recall rather than a database lookup; I know of no evidence linking it to regulation of cholesterol transport.

I recognise this sequence as human STING (STING1/TMEM173), an ER transmembrane adaptor of the cGAS pathway; from recalled literature rather than anything derived here, cholesterol-recognition (CRAC) motifs in STING have been reported to bind cholesterol directly and control its ER retention, so the term plausibly applies, though with moderate confidence.

This is human STING (STING1/TMEM173), which I recognise from the sequence; its recalled localisations are ER, ERGIC, Golgi, perinuclear vesicle, autophagosome and lysosomal membranes, and although it is degraded via lysosomes I do not recall a specific endolysosome membrane annotation, so this is a moderately confident no.

This sequence is human STING (STING1/TMEM173); from my recollection of recent structural work, PtdIns(3,5)P2 was reported to bind STING directly and promote its oligomerization and activation alongside cGAMP, though I am recalling this rather than deriving it from the sequence.

The sequence is human STING1 (TMEM173), a multi-pass ER/Golgi membrane adaptor in cGAS–cyclic dinucleotide innate immune signalling; as far as I recall, its localisation annotations are ER, Golgi, vesicle and autophagosome membranes rather than chromatin, despite some reports of a nuclear envelope pool.

The sequence is human STING (STING1/TMEM173), an ER membrane adaptor that binds cyclic dinucleotides such as 2'3'-cGAMP and signals through TBK1/IRF3; it is not an enzyme and has no adenylate-forming or CoA-ligase domain that would give acid-thiol ligase activity.

This sequence is human STING (STING1/TMEM173), a four-transmembrane ER adaptor that binds cyclic dinucleotides such as 2',3'-cGAMP in innate immune signalling; it is not a seven-transmembrane GPCR, and bile acid receptor activity belongs to GPBAR1/TGR5.

This sequence looks like human PLD5 (inactive phospholipase D5), a single-pass transmembrane, glycosylated PLD3/4-like protein of the secretory/endolysosomal membrane system, with no known chromatin association.

The sequence appears to be human inactive phospholipase D5 (PLD5), a single-pass membrane protein of the PLD3/PLD4 family; from recall, it has no known ciliary tip localisation, which is typical of IFT and Hedgehog-pathway proteins instead.

The sequence looks like human ULK4, a catalytically inactive pseudokinase with a long C-terminal armadillo/HEAT-repeat region; from recalled literature (not derived from the sequence itself) it is reported to scaffold STK36/Fused with Gli2 in Hedgehog signalling and cilia, which fits an adaptor role.

The sequence appears to be human ULK4, a pseudokinase that, as I recall from published work, partners with STK36/Fused and promotes Sonic hedgehog signalling by supporting STK36 ciliary localisation and Gli2 phosphorylation; this is from memory of the literature, not derived from the sequence alone.

The sequence appears to be ERLEC1 (XTP3-B), an endoplasmic reticulum lumenal lectin with a signal peptide and two MRH domains that acts in ER-associated degradation, not a nuclear transcription elongation factor complex component.

This is human MYD88, a death-domain/TIR-domain adaptor for Toll-like and IL-1 receptor signalling in innate immunity; it has no known role in transcription-coupled nucleotide-excision repair.

This appears to be human POPDC2, a cAMP-binding Popeye domain membrane protein known mainly for roles in cardiac pacemaking and conduction and in striated muscle; from recall, I know of no evidence linking it to glucose-stimulated insulin secretion.

This sequence appears to be human POPDC2, a Popeye domain-containing cAMP-binding membrane protein of striated muscle, not a mitochondrial carrier; mitochondrial CoA transport is carried out by SLC25 family members such as SLC25A42 and SLC25A16.
